Every year I give my students a case and ask them who should win, and every year they start in the wrong place. The first question in international law is not who is right. It is whether the court has jurisdiction. National courts have jurisdiction almost automatically: if you live in a country, its courts can judge you. International courts are different. A state is judged only if it has agreed to be judged, and that consent can be given in a treaty, in a special agreement, or in a declaration made years before the dispute began. So when a court says it has no jurisdiction, it is not saying the state was innocent. It is saying that the question was never allowed into the room. Remember that distinction, because it appears in almost every exam I write.

Listeners often ask us a fair question. If an international court orders a country to do something, and the country simply does not do it, what happens next? The honest answer is that there is no international police that arrives at the border. Enforcement works in quieter ways. A ruling that is ignored damages the reputation of the government that ignores it, and other states remember that in their next negotiation. Some courts send the case to a political body, which can put diplomatic pressure on the state. And inside the country, lawyers and judges often use the international ruling to change national law, one case at a time. Researchers who study these courts say that full compliance is rare, but partial compliance is common, and it often arrives years after the ruling.
